title: Escalating cross-border insecurity linked to the Sudan conflict increases protection risks and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Since early 2026, the conflict in Sudan has evolved from a humanitarian crisis affecting Chad into a direct security threat to eastern border areas. Repeated drone strikes, cross-border incursions, and clashes involving fighters aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have already caused casualties on Chadian territory, including around Tine and other border regions. These incidents indicate a growing risk that the Sudan conflict could generate sustained military confrontations, proxy violence, or retaliatory attacks inside Chad. This risk is increasingly characterised by the possibility of sustained military confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces operating along the Chad–Sudan border.

This risk is driven by a convergence of security, economic, and political factors. The Chad–Sudan border has become a strategic corridor for the movement of fuel, arms, gold, and military supplies supporting groups involved in the Sudan conflict. Competition over these routes has transformed border areas into contested spaces where violence increasingly follows smuggling and supply networks. Recent attacks suggest a shift from incidental spillover to deliberate projection of force into Chadian territory.

The conflict is also aggravating existing vulnerabilities in Chad. Fractures within cross-border Zaghawa community networks, which remain influential within Chad’s security apparatus, have deepened as communities react to violence in Darfur and perceptions of Chad’s involvement in the conflict. Continued violence in Darfur, combined with Chad’s historical role in Sudanese proxy conflicts, increases the risk of elite defections, armed realignments, and renewed cross-border mobilisation. Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may also re-emerge, including support to armed groups and militias operating across the border, increasing the likelihood of retaliatory attacks and further regional destabilisation.

Over the next one to three months, further RSF incursions, SAF-backed proxy activity, or competition over border corridors could increase cross-border violence, displacement, protection risks, and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad. Additional attacks or retaliations would likely worsen conditions in provinces already hosting large numbers of refugees and returnees, further straining regional services, humanitarian operations, and community relations. The risk is not limited to humanitarian spillover and increasingly involves the possibility of sustained confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces. ([Africa Center for Strategic Studies 09/03/2026](https://africacenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Chad-Risks-Instability.pdf), [ACLED 08/04/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/africa-overview-april-2026), [Global Initiative 06/03/2026](https://globalinitiative.net/analysis/how-border-criminal-economies-are-drawing-chad-further-into-sudans-conflict/), [ISS Africa 03/04/2025](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/urgent-au-action-could-defuse-rising-chad-sudan-tensions), [RFI 13/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260513-tchad-de-nouvelles-frappes-enregistr%C3%A9es-%C3%A0-la-fronti%C3%A8re-soudanaise-font-craindre-le-pire), [UNHCR 18/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/core-emergency-situation-chad-update-arrivals-sudan-17-may-2026), [UNFPA 15/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/unfpa-situation-report-chad-humanitarian-response-1-30-april-2026))

triggers.title: Expansion of cross-border attacks and insecurity
triggers.description: :Additional drone strikes, shelling, or armed incursions near the Chad–Sudan border, particularly around Adré, Tina, and other eastern border localities, increase civilian casualties, trigger further displacement into Chad, and constrain humanitarian operations in already fragile border areas. Continued insecurity may also disrupt cross-border trade and movement routes relied upon by refugees and host communities Sources: ([UNFPA 30/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/unfpa-situation-report-chad-humanitarian-response-1-30-april-2026\), [RFI 13/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260513-tchad-de-nouvelles-frappes-enregistr%C3%A9es-%C3%A0-la-fronti%C3%A8re-soudanaise-font-craindre-le-pire\), [FEWS NET 22/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/chad-food-security-outlook-update-refugee-impacts-are-driving-income-and-consumption-toward-crisis-ipc-phase-3-april-september-2026\)) Completion rate: 40% Completion rate history: 02-06-2026: 40% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Yes. 100% completion would be reached if cross-border attacks become sustained and recurrent, affecting multiple border localities in eastern Chad and causing significant civilian casualties, displacement, or humanitarian access disruptions. triggers.title: Attacks on strategic infrastructure in Chad
triggers.description: Threats by Sudanese actors against Chadian airports, border facilities, military positions, or transport infrastructure may materialise into direct attacks on strategic assets in eastern Chad. Any strike against airports such as Amdjarass, military installations, or critical transport corridors would increase the risk of direct confrontation between Chad and Sudanese armed actors, disrupt humanitarian and commercial operations, and further destabilise border regions Sources: ([ISS Africa 31/03/2026](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/urgent-au-action-could-defuse-rising-chad-sudan-tensions\), [ACLED 08/04/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/africa-overview-april-2026\), [Africa Center 09/03/2026](https://africacenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Chad-Risks-Instability.pdf\)) Completion rate: 10% Completion rate history: 02-06-2026: 20% 02-06-2026: 10% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Yes. 100% completion would be reached if attacks directly target strategic infrastructure in Chad, including airports, military facilities, border posts, or major transport corridors, causing significant disruption to civilian, humanitarian, or commercial activities. Trend: Trend history: Date entered: 02-06-2026 Last update: 08-06-2026

triggers.title: Renewed proxy mobilisation and cross-border armed group activity
triggers.description: Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may re-emerge through the mobilisation, arming, or support of rebel groups and allied militias operating along the border. Increased involvement of SAF-aligned groups, RSF-linked actors, Darfuri armed factions, or Chadian rebel networks could expand the conflict beyond isolated border incidents and increase the likelihood of retaliatory attacks on Chadian territory. Sources: ([ISS Africa 31/03/2026](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/urgent-au-action-could-defuse-rising-chad-sudan-tensions\), [Africa Center 09/03/2026](https://africacenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Chad-Risks-Instability.pdf\), [Global Initiative 06/03/2026](https://globalinitiative.net/analysis/how-border-criminal-economies-are-drawing-chad-further-into-sudans-conflict/\)) Completion rate: 20% Completion rate history: 02-06-2026: 20% Quantitative objective to meet 100%: Yes. 100% completion would be reached if armed groups, militias, or proxy actors operating across the Chad–Sudan border become actively involved in cross-border hostilities, resulting in sustained violence, retaliatory attacks, or territorial insecurity in eastern Chad.
